In addition, there is a need for “more diverse training and testing sets for AI algorithm development and refinement” across different races and ethnicities, said Christoph Lee, director of the Northwest Screening and Cancer Outcomes Research Enterprise at the University of Washington School of Medicine.
The long shadow of an earlier and largely unsuccessful type of computer-assisted mammography hangs over the adoption of newer AI tools. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, “computer-assisted detection” software promised to improve breast cancer detection. Then the studies started coming in, and the results were often far from encouraging. Using CAD at best provided no benefit, and at worst reduced the accuracy of radiologists’ interpretations, resulting in higher rates of recalls and biopsies.
“CAD was not that sophisticated,” said Robert Smith, senior vice president of early cancer detection science at the American Cancer Society. Artificial intelligence tools today are a whole different ballgame, he said. “You can train the algorithm to pick up things, or it learns on its own.”
Smith said he found it “troubling” that radiologists would charge for the AI analysis.
“There are too many women who can’t afford any out-of-pocket cost” for a mammogram, Smith said. “If we’re not going to increase the number of radiologists we use for mammograms, then these new AI tools are going to be very useful, and I don’t think we can defend charging women extra for them.”

title: Council Post: The Future Of AI In Business
text:
Laura Scotti is the CEO of ScottiWorks on behalf of Pathways Consulting Group.
Generative AI has broken into the world of business in a big way. The public release of ChatGPT in late 2022 swiftly popularized this new technology across various industries, touching on everything from finance to technology.
In many ways, the scale of its impact far exceeded expectations, ushering in a global revolution that has the potential to reshape the way we live and work, and in my opinion, is akin to the transformative power of the internet.
As I look at AI's impact, I am excited to explore its possibilities and encourage other business leaders to attempt to understand its potential uses. While the speed of technological advancements continues to increase, it simultaneously becomes vital for organizations to remain at the forefront of these changes. The ramifications of falling behind can be disastrous.
Here, I will explore AI and the promises, predictions and potential pitfalls that lie ahead as AI continues to evolve.
Unfolding Potential For The Future
The projections for growth are nothing short of staggering. According to Statista, the AI industry has doubled in the past two years. That level of exponential growth is expected to continue for the foreseeable future. Even conservative estimates predict the industry to be worth nearly $2 trillion by 2030. This exponential growth pattern is a decent representation of what we can expect to see regarding public adoption of AI—a paradigm shift that will fundamentally alter the way we play, work and think.
AI Versus Generative AI
Traditional AI, also called narrow AI, refers to a programming algorithm. They are used in data analysis, video games and email filtering. These programs use various algorithms, such as decision trees, expert systems and natural language processing (NLP) systems to predict outcomes based on previous data.
Generative AI is the next step. These models are trained on vast amounts of data and rely on machine learning to understand information. As a result, they can generate new content that follows similar patterns. For example, the predictive text on your phone uses narrow AI. The information supplied tells the program the most likely words you will choose next. Generative AI, however, can take samples of writing and create entirely new content from the ground up.
Enhancing Workplace Development And Growth
As AI continues its rapid evolution, organizations that incorporate it have an opportunity to gain significant advantages. Prominent platforms such as ServiceNow, Sprout Social and Supernormal leverage AI in unique ways to enhance user’s productivity and efficiency. Each of these tools is designed to meet different organizational requirements. Regardless of the objectives of a specific tool, best practices recommend training the AI and adjusting prompts to most accurately mimic the tone, style and output representative of your organization.
By utilizing real-time data analysis and analytics, organizations can promptly respond to market fluctuations and seize emerging opportunities. The predictive abilities of AI tools allow organizations to adapt to evolving consumer behavior, gaining a competitive edge.
Preparing For The AI Era
Like any new technology, AI comes with a learning curve. While trial and error are part of the process, partnering with an experienced partner can help speed it up. Working with a reputable group can make a significant difference in your ROI.
Consultants and experts can provide integration, training and customized solutions, allowing your staff to utilize the technology more quickly. AI has different uses, including data analysis, content creation, graphic design and even technical support. Therefore, adequate training is critical for efficient implementation.
AI-Driven Content
Generative AI is currently utilized by major platforms such as Amazon, creating a concise summary of customer reviews. This trend is emerging elsewhere and will continue, including the application of generative AI within workflow programs such as Now Assist by ServiceNow. This program facilitates similar summaries for items like conversations and help tickets, allowing representatives to generate an easy, understandable synopsis of customer complaints.
Social media management platforms like Sprout Social, with its amalgamation of data analytics and content creation, allow users to generate content faster, easier and with more personalization than ever before.
Workflow Automation And Efficiency
Despite AI’s capabilities, the majority of today’s "busy work" still relies on manual completion. With this next generation of AI, however, organizations can pinpoint their most repetitive, mundane tasks and set them aside for automation. AI tools can be trained to assist with or even fully take over these jobs, allowing more time to be directed to activities that contribute to business growth. This, in turn, ensures more efficient processes and reduces unnecessary busy work for key staff.
Perfect Fit Hiring
The current AI programs used in human resources are primarily keyword-dependent algorithms. Generative AI allows for a more advanced approach that goes beyond specific keywords to include synonyms and related skills.
It may have the capacity to integrate industry-specific AIs directly related to a given industry or job and generate screening questions specific to the company and position. Coupled with personalized communication and outreach campaigns, HR AIs can help you target individuals with the skills, location and need for the vacant position.
Warnings And Ethical Considerations
While the promises of AI feel limitless, it is important to acknowledge the challenges associated with its rapid advancement and adoption. AI is susceptible to biases, both from online sources and individuals, which can and should raise concerns regarding fairness, accountability and accuracy. AI, like other technology, should be seen as a tool to enhance work, not a replacement for the human elements in the work itself.
As we navigate AI’s integration into our daily world, excitement for the future continues to grow. The potential for technological advancements feels limitless. However, as the initial stewards of this technology, we must approach AI with a commitment to ethical use, and an expectation that the future will remain unpredictable, no matter how advanced our technology becomes.

title: Council Post: A Tidal Wave Of Financial Empowerment Is Coming
text:
Adam is the Founder and CEO of Domain Money.
I’ve seen firsthand inside the belly of our financial system. And I can tell you that it’s designed to take advantage of the little guy.
Let’s start with banking. Dodd-Frank and the Durbin Amendment that followed were designed to introduce more competition in the lending market. In response, banks simply hiked their fees, more than making up for the shortfall in interest revenue. The results speak for themselves. Profits among the big six consumer banks have soared.
Consumers still pay exorbitant rates to borrow, on average 11.56% for personal loans as of Jan. 3, 2024, (if they can secure one) and often over 25% for credit card debt. Over a quarter of consumers with checking accounts pay banks $288 each year simply for the privilege of accessing their money, even though overall consumers earn a pittance on their deposits. The national average for savings deposits was sitting at 0.47% APY as of Jan. 16, 2024, despite short-term U.S. Treasury bills paying over 5%.
What’s worse is that overdraft and non-sufficient funds charges make up almost two-thirds of all fee revenue among the largest banks. It’s these punitive charges that hit the most economically vulnerable the hardest, with nearly 80% of all overdraft fees coming from less than 10% of customer accounts.
The story is no better with insurance. A study by the Kaiser Family Foundation found that carriers participating in the Affordable Care Act denied coverage for in-network claims up to 49% of the time, with an overall denial rate of roughly 17%. Meanwhile, consumers appealed less than two-tenths of 1% of denied in-network claims, and the majority of those denials were upheld on appeal. Doesn’t seem fair, does it? Given the complexity of the appeal process, most consumers simply accept whatever coverage they get.
Boosting Financial Empowerment With Online Tools
Despite the efforts of organizations such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the rules promulgated by the Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act, the average consumer has little power against banks or insurance companies to improve the hand they’ve been dealt.
The internet has unleashed a transformational wave of tools enabling individuals to do something about this asymmetry of power. Comparison sites such as NerdWallet enable consumers to shop for the lowest rates to borrow, and tools like CreditKarma help consumers stay on top of their credit scores, improving their chances of a better deal. But these tools are just the beginning.
Here are a few examples. The way credit bureaus calculate your credit score is a “black box,” mostly a mystery to consumers. But companies like Self have figured out ways to automate improving credit scores for consumers. Max is a service that helps you optimize your deposits among banks to ensure you get the highest interest rate possible. And Billshark can negotiate to get you a better deal on services such as internet and cable.
Going Even Further With AI
This wave of consumer advocacy tools is an enormous improvement, but it’s about to be weaponized by generative artificial intelligence in ways that will transform the market.
Take a robo-caller, add generative AI and direct it to negotiate with your insurance company. It could learn how to best negotiate with your insurance company for a specific kind of claim, at scale.
And it’s the at-scale part that is most interesting. In the first few weeks after ChatGPT launched, it passed exams for both the medical and legal professions. Highly specialized fields can be quickly mastered by AI, so imagine its power directed at consumer advocacy.
While those who can afford it may want a human with a law degree to fight with their insurance company or bank, for the majority of consumers who can’t afford to fight, or don’t know how, an AI-powered advocate is a godsend. Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, which offers ChatGPT free to consumers and is the fastest-growing application in internet history, said it well: “AI is going to be the greatest force for economic empowerment.”
What many don’t appreciate about generative AI is how quickly it can learn about you specifically and cross reference data in ways no one individual could. I expect that one day soon, you’ll be able to ask AI to review your medical records and DNA and recommend an insurance plan best suited for you.
Where else in the world could a consumer get that kind of insight? What doctor or insurance agent today could possibly provide it?
Similarly, one day soon you’ll likely be able to ask AI to compare the fees you pay your bank against the interest they pay you, or rationalize the performance of two investment funds that use different performance or accounting methodologies.
Turning The Tables
While much of the debate about AI has focused on what jobs will be eliminated or whether it’s safe, it’s my view these tools will meaningfully level the playing field anywhere powerful institutions take advantage of the little guy. For decades, large companies have used big data and machine learning to squeeze an extra dollar out of consumers’ pockets. Now, these tools, and more powerful ones that will emerge from the collective wisdom of generative AI, will be unleashed against those same institutions.
It’s a bit like Prometheus stealing fire from the gods. It will herald a wave of consumer empowerment unlike anything we’ve ever seen. As the great social commentators Public Enemy so presciently said, “fight the powers that be.” With AI on their side, consumers finally can.

title: Council Post: All Hype? How To Counter Distrust In AI By Looking Under The Hood
text:
Syed Ahmed is SVP of Engineering at Act-On Software, a leading marketing automation platform.
AI adoption is rising across businesses worldwide, accompanied by a mix of hype, excitement and hesitation. But without AI-driven outcomes that are both reliable and predictable, it can be difficult to gain trust in this booming sector. By understanding how AI features come to their conclusions, one can better fine-tune them to deliver optimum results from a foundation of trust.
If AI tools make suggestions, users need those suggestions to be accurate and to yield helpful results. Across many sectors, users can’t afford even small AI mistakes. To highlight this, in an August 2023 CFP Board survey, 51% of users said they had "little or no trust in financial advice" provided by AI.
In 2012, the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center used IBM’s Watson supercomputer in hopes to better personalize oncology treatment based on patient preferences. But it often gave patients incorrect advice due to an overreliance on theoretical data instead of metrics from real patients. One example was when "it suggested a cancer patient with severe bleeding be given a drug that could cause bleeding to worsen." If such advice were followed, it would have catastrophic results. Eventually, this collaboration was canceled.
In 2021, Zillow relied on iBuying’s AI algorithms to buy and sell houses. Unfortunately, the algorithm was incorrect for Q3 and Q4, resulting in Zillow overpaying for homes. This overpayment combined with overtly aggressive expansion led to stunning losses of over $550 million. What seemed to be an easy solution ended up being a huge mess.
When AI lets users down in this way, it leaves a lasting impression of distrust. And if users don’t have trust, what do they have? As theologian Isaac Watts put it, “Learning to trust is one of life’s most difficult tasks.” Even one negative experience—no matter how small—can lead people to think twice about ever using a feature again for important tasks. Ideally, AI should lead users toward a solution along the lines of what they would think of themselves.
So, how do we develop deeper trust in AI solutions? The first step is to broaden the understanding of AI utility. When looking at an AI-supported feature, think about how it comes to its conclusions. Maybe it’s tailoring a solution based on your past proven successes. It could be combining business trends with proven predictive formulae. Whether AI is powering a little or a lot of your app, it’s worth learning how it gets there. Transparency about how a system works can lead to greater trust and increased usage. Some organizations have harnessed AI to great effect, both from a user and business perspective.
Google Ads manages to deliver custom ads to users based on their search history and sites they’ve visited. The more an ad is tailored to the user, the more likely they’ll engage with it. According to a study featured on e-commerce Fastlane, 80% of customers “desire the personalized touch of Google Ads tailored to their specific locale.”
Netflix uses AI and people’s viewing history to personalize and determine what movies or shows to recommend next. This extends not just to titles but also to the hyper-specific categories (moody action-adventure) and even to the specific thumbnail images displayed. Many movies use several different cover art options to appeal to different audiences based on viewing habits. For example, if you’ve been watching a lot of romantic comedies, thumbnail images might focus on couples in the film rather than individual movie stars.
When using AI in these ways to drive marketing and engagement, it’s crucial to use specificity to generate more accurate metrics for each user and achieve a positive impact on business objectives. A Harvard Business Review article (paywall) posits that when linking AI prediction with a business outcome, it’s worth evaluating the AI’s accuracy against the desired results. To achieve this, it’s important that “marketing and data science teams answer this together.” Therefore, AI can help persuade customers through greater trust if you’re willing to work with it.
The more control one has over their AI model, the more confidence they'll have in using it. Although it can be a long road to get there, the destination is worth the reward, with AI hype being flipped into a well-deserved celebration and adoption.

title: Council Post: Five Techniques To Ensure Reliable And Honest Use Of Generative AI
text:
President & CTO at ContractPodAi.
It's no longer a stretch of the imagination to see how generative artificial intelligence (AI) brings value to modern enterprises. Streamlined work speeds up organizational processes, accurate collection of data reduces human errors and advanced analytics facilitates strategic decision-making.
With senior leaders, business users and customers becoming more aware of these benefits, the deployment of the technology within organizations is happening at a rapid pace. In 2022 alone, according to research published by Statista, large-scale generative AI adoption was more than 20%; by 2025, it is expected to reach nearly 50%.
Nevertheless, it's important for companies to take a breath and a step back amid this wave of adoption in the corporate workplace. Early adopters of technology of this caliber often reap significant benefits, and there's much urgency to adopt this as a means of getting ahead competitively and increasing operational efficiencies.
However, early adopters must be prepared for unexpected outcomes and be ready to make adjustments as the technology continues to evolve. The implementation process will determine the success of generative AI, and a well-thought-through approach is essential.
Below are five ways to ensure reliable (and honest) use of generative AI for your business today and in the future.
Apply A Foundational Layer For AI
First, the output of the AI system should make sense for the task and, more broadly, your industry. For instance, if you are using generative AI for legal purposes, make certain that the system is only generating high-quality outputs that are relevant to legal departments and users.
Tailoring the output toward the specific industry helps build trust and mitigates the risk of outputting irrelevant content. This helps drive better business outcomes in the present but also plays a large role in contributing to shaping the application and direction of AI technology moving forward.
Trust, But Verify
Generative AI's insights and suggestions should be considered as supplementary resources instead of a substitute for human knowledge. It's important for users to be aware that this technology (and any technology in general) can occasionally produce inaccuracies; therefore, generative AI should be treated as a "supportive copilot" instead of an autonomous agent.
The system's outputs should be thoroughly reviewed rather than looked at as a substitute for human review and decision-making. Additionally, while AI can process data, we must be mindful that this technology lacks human contextual understanding and be aware of the wider context when interpreting and applying its outputs.
Be Prepared To Troubleshoot
Despite generative AI's potential for enhancing business operations globally, one potential flaw of the technology is what's known as a "hallucination," where the large language models (LLMs) may tend to generate inaccurate or unexpected outputs. When faced with this, users can try different prompt formulations or redraft the prompt in alternative ways and resubmit it for improved results. Always cross-verify information and be aware of this inherent aspect of AI systems.
Raise Organizational Awareness
By helping users understand the proverbial "do's and don'ts" of AI and the limitations of its usage, they will then be more comfortable engaging with this technology and trusting it. In other words, better AI literacy leads to more informed decisions about the technology's usage and increased engagement with AI-generated content.
Legal teams and HR leaders should prepare policies and training on using generative AI and new technologies, ensuring that team members throughout the organization are aware of the benefits and negatives of using such tools.
Increase Technical Supervision Of AI And Its Users
Without proper controls and oversight, generative AI can have a negative impact on the business. Think about the proliferation of unsafe, inaccurate or out-of-date information. To combat this, administrators can put into place permissions as to who can access AI-generated content as well as establish parameters and rules around the types of outputs the AI can—and cannot—deliver. This serves to provide strict control over user and system actions as well as enterprise security.
As generative AI models become more widespread in industries, the technology's adoption calls for the critical steps mentioned above and other best practices.
Implementing proper frameworks and guardrails around the technology will go a long way toward preventing the dissemination of unsound information and the misuse of systems altogether. This added level of security will create trust among senior leaders, business users and customers—those who are cautious about deploying the latest digital tools and taking advantage of their inherent capabilities.

title: Council Post: Navigating The AI Era: The Rise Of Personalized, Real-Time E-Commerce Experiences
text:
Kuk is the cofounder of ZEGOCLOUD, a global cloud communication service provider of real-time audio and video communication APIs and SDKs.
Covid-19 has brought unprecedented impacts to all walks of life. The e-commerce industry has become one of the few that can actively adapt and benefit from it. Traditional business models are also trying to re-engineer to embrace and thrive on e-commerce.
With the rapid growth of e-shopping and the ever-evolving consumer expectations, AI-powered technologies—including real-time communication, real-time interaction (a more sophisticated variation of RTC) and AI-generated content—have emerged as powerful tools to enhance the overall e-commerce experience.
The Surge Of E-Commerce And AI Integration
In the International Trade Administration Report, the e-commerce share of total global retail sales experienced a substantial boost during the epidemic, with an 8% increase from 13.6% in 2019 to 21.1% in 2023.
The Covid-19 epidemic has not only changed people's shopping behavior and consumption habits but also significantly affected the e-commerce landscape, pushing businesses to adopt AI-powered technologies to meet consumers' changing needs and expectations. Real-time communication, real-time interaction, AI-generated content and other innovative technologies have proven powerful tools in enhancing the overall e-commerce experience. As the e-commerce industry continues to evolve, AI will play an even more significant role in shaping the future of online shopping.
Leveraging AI For Enhanced Real-Time Engagement In E-Commerce
AI is revolutionizing e-commerce by facilitating live interactions, providing personalized services and generating user-focused content.
• Live product demonstrations and advice: Video calls or real-time chat allow merchants to provide real-time product demonstrations and advice. Digital humans, powered by AI, are becoming the new face of live streaming, allowing companies to create virtual live streams without human presenters, equipment or venues. Virtual host live streaming is freed from the limitations of many factors, such as an unguaranteed schedule, high hiring costs, expensive traffic and venue or equipment costs.
• Instantaneous customer support: Real-time interactive tools (such as online chat or voice calls) allow users to communicate with merchant representatives or customer support teams in real time to provide immediate assistance and answer questions. This feature enhances the user experience, facilitates rapid problem resolution and increases user confidence in purchase decisions. For example, VEED.IO uses the latest AI technology to create compelling videos that can be used for different business needs, such as selling or marketing presentations, which drives brand engagement and direct sales through real-time interactions.
• Personalized recommendations and customization: Through real-time interaction, merchants can communicate with users and understand their needs to provide personalized product recommendations and customized services. Merchants can tailor recommended goods or services in real time based on user preferences and needs, increasing satisfaction and purchase intent. Amazon is at the forefront of e-commerce personalization. It uses AI algorithms to personalize product recommendations, search results and marketing emails based on browsing and purchase history.
E-Commerce Development Trends With AI Technology
The future of AI technology in e-commerce is exciting. As technology advances and consumer needs change, AI technology will play an increasingly important role. The integration of real-time communication, real-time interaction, AI-generated content (AIGC) and digital humans is shaping the future of e-commerce. Here are some of the trends emerging from the convergence of these technologies.
• Enhanced video calls with digital representatives: E-commerce platforms are integrating RTC and enhancing it with AI to provide seamless real-time interactions. Video calls are now powered by AI-driven digital representatives who can handle product inquiries, provide support and facilitate transactions with a human-like touch. This AI-personalized communication marries the convenience of online shopping with the bespoke service traditionally found in physical retail.
• Automated, real-time content creation: E-commerce thrives on content. AI-generated content (AIGC) revolutionizes how e-commerce platforms manage and produce content. Beyond simple automation, these systems leverage intelligence to craft product descriptions, reviews and promotional materials that are both high in quality and personalized and dynamically updated in response to inventory and consumer behavior changes. This real-time content adaptation ensures that the information customers see is always relevant and tailored to their needs.
• Predictive customer service with AI Insights: The fusion of RTC with predictive analytics allows digital humans to anticipate customer needs and preferences. AI can forecast trends such as purchase timing and product preferences by analyzing customer interactions and data. E-commerce sites can thus proactively adjust their customer service, offering highly personalized support and recommendations that improve the shopping experience and foster brand loyalty.
Precautions For Business Owners
While embracing AI, business owners still need to be mindful of the following aspects.
• Data privacy and security: As AI handles large amounts of customer data, ensure robust privacy policies and security measures are in place to protect sensitive information.
• Ethical considerations: Digital humans and AI representatives should be disclosed to customers to avoid misleading them about the nature of the interaction.
• Accuracy and reliability: AI systems should be continuously trained and tested to ensure accuracy in personalization and recommendations. Monitor AI interactions to prevent potential errors that could lead to customer dissatisfaction or miscommunication.
• Technological investment: Evaluate the cost and ROI of implementing AI technologies, as they may require significant initial investment in money, time and training.
• Continuous evaluation and adaptation: Regularly evaluate the performance of AI tools and be ready to adapt strategies in response to technological advancements and changing consumer behaviors.
Conclusion
As the e-commerce industry forges ahead in this AI-augmented era, it is evident that AI-enhanced real-time communication (RTC) will be pivotal in driving forward the paradigm shift toward a more interactive, personalized and efficient online shopping journey. By wielding the potential of AI, businesses can transcend traditional barriers, offering consumers unprecedented convenience and connection.
However, as we chart this new territory, innovators and entrepreneurs must navigate with foresight and responsibility—ensuring that these advancements elevate user experiences and uphold the highest privacy, ethics, and inclusivity standards. The future beckons with a promise of AI-empowered commerce, where every digital interaction is an opportunity to delight, engage and build lasting consumer relationships. We must respond to this call with the prudence and ingenuity that will define the next chapter of e-commerce.

title: Deloitte BrandVoice: Bearing The Load: How Can Power And Utilities Companies Prepare For Accelerating Demand?
text:
Managing the accelerating electricity demand is a pervasive challenge in transforming the grid. Recent reports have suggested that global electricity demand is expected to rise by 5 900 terawatt-hours (TWh) in the Stated Energy Policies Scenario (STEPS) and over 7,000 TWh in the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) by 2030—equivalent to adding the current level of demand in the United States and the European Union. Electrification, which is necessary for reducing emissions, is the driving force behind much of this anticipated increase.
Expanding end-uses for electricity
Electrification of the transportation, building, and industrial segments continues to pick up speed in many parts of the world. In the transportation segment, electric vehicle (EV) adoption rates are surpassing expectations in some regions. In the US, for instance, EV sales are expected to reach nearly 9% of new car sales in 2023, which is beyond what many consider a “tipping point” for mass adoption—and they’re likely to pass the one million cars per year milestone before the end of 2023.
Electrification may also be accelerating in the building segment as residential and commercial buildings move to electric heat pumps and water heaters instead of fossil-fueled systems. This trend has been particularly pronounced in Europe, which documented record heat pump sales in 2022, with around 3 million units sold. Rising computing demands from data centers using digital technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain are also lifting demand. As one of the most energy-intensive building types, these data centers consume 10 to 50 times the energy per square foot compared to standard office buildings.
While making progress, the industrial segment may be the slowest to electrify since upfront capital costs to electrify industrial processes are generally higher than those for switching to low-carbon alternative fuels such as clean hydrogen or ammonia, and payback periods are often longer. In addition, electric heating technologies are currently better suited for low- and medium-temperature processes, and often require new equipment and workforce retraining.
Funding the energy transition
Amid an inflationary environment in many parts of the world, power and utility companies are being challenged to balance growing capital expenditures with customer affordability. Costs are mounting to upgrade and modernize the grid, harden it against severe weather, prepare for rising demand, and source more renewable energy. Depending upon the regulatory scheme, some of these costs may be passed on to end-users via rate hikes. But, after the recent electricity crisis in Europe and record residential price hikes in the US in 2022, utility regulators may be more likely to challenge and limit rate increases.
One variable to watch is fuel costs. Wholesale natural gas price declines can flow through to customer electric bills, often through automatic fuel adjustment clauses, which can help offset other increases in the bill. But the reverse can also happen when fuel costs rise.
In addition to rate increases, utilities will likely continue to tap alternative sources to raise cash for their capital programs and keep customer bills affordable. These may include grants, loans, and tax credits from government programs; as well as operational savings, asset sales, and business model innovations.
Digital transformation as an enabler
Another lever to pull in pursuit of affordability is digital transformation. While the growth in data centers can drive demand, new digital advancements can also drive savings. Some companies are also planning to divert savings from business transformation programs into their capital spending programs. For example, many electric companies are generating efficiencies through digital technologies such as smart grid, digital customer service platforms, and outage maintenance optimization. These benefits may be just the beginning. The power sector is on the verge of entering a transformative era, led by AI including Generative AI (GenAI), a subset of AI that when prompted, creates new content in the form of text, code, voice, images, videos, and processes.
In the long-term, AI, including GenAI, has the potential to help address core power industry challenges such as:
- Grid management and optimization: Power distribution and transmission can be optimized by considering factors such as load balancing, congestion management, and asset utilization.
- Resource management and planning: AI will likely excel in generating accurate electricity demand forecasts and enabling streamlined resource allocation. It could also help optimize solar panel and wind turbine designs by analyzing local factors such as weather patterns, solar radiation, and wind speed.
- Operational efficiency and reliability: As AI advances, it will likely enable the industry to further automate tasks, predict and prevent equipment failures, and enhance network reliability, ensuring more seamless operations.
Electrification across end-use sectors may accelerate in 2024 and beyond, buoying longer term electric power industry forecasts and impacting strategies. In addition, the industry will likely sharpen its focus on resource adequacy concerns amid grid transformation. Accordingly, power and utilities companies will likely continue to seek new ways to address rising costs, with digital transformation being front and center as a potential solution. This includes exploring whether AI, including GenAI, could be part of their approach to bearing the load — and ultimately to enhancing reliability, sustainability, and affordability throughout the power and utilities sector.

title: Council Post: 14 Ways To Create Unique Marketing And Ad Campaigns With AI
text:
The rise of publicly accessible generative artificial intelligence tools has dominated conversations in both the media and executive conference rooms over the past year. While consumers and business leaders alike try to wrap their heads around the implications of this massive technological evolution, marketers and advertisers are enthusiastically embracing their roles as early adopters of generative AI.
Below, members of Forbes Agency Council share ideas for melding generative AI with content and campaigns in authentic ways to create unique marketing and advertising creatives. Read on for innovative and actionable insights into how brands can leverage AI to better reach target audiences.
1. Host Co-Creation Events
Hosting community events where participants co-create content with AI can be an exciting way to engage the audience. For instance, a brand could organize an event where people submit ideas or themes, and then AI generates creative interpretations of those concepts. This not only fosters community engagement, but also results in diverse and original content. - Azad Abbasi, Genius XR
2. Create Interactive Ads
Incorporating AI into interactive ads can create more engaging and immersive consumer experiences. For example, an AI-powered ad could change based on user interactions, or it could use augmented reality to blend the digital and physical worlds. - Cagan Sean Yuksel, Dreamspace
3. Revise Old Campaigns
Using generative AI is a great way to revise old campaigns for new audiences. Using AI to analyze successful blog articles, social media posts, ads, emails and more to create new content personas, for example, is one quick way to jump-start marketing team brainstorms and enable scalable results. - Vix Reitano, Agency 6B
4. Explore AI-Driven Interactive Experiences
AI-driven interactive experiences could involve chatbots, augmented reality or other interactive elements that enhance user engagement and provide a unique and memorable brand experience. By incorporating interactive elements, you can take a dynamic and multifaceted approach to your content marketing strategy. - Ivonna Young, The Lavender Agency
5. Craft Personalized Visuals And Dynamic Copy
Infuse generative AI into marketing by crafting personalized visuals and dynamic copy. Leverage AI to analyze user preferences and generate tailored content that resonates. Break free from clichés with AI-curated imagery and language, ensuring a fresh, engaging brand experience. - Ajay Prasad, GMR Web Team

6. Give Content, Images And Video A Second Life
Generative AI can give content, images and video a second life—much like taking bits of salvaged glass to create a mosaic—transforming what may have been a relic (lackluster copy or an unusable or static image), reviving it, and turning it into something new and unique. A broken vase (old copy) may seem destined for the landfill, but with some creativity (AI), it can become a work of art. - Thomas Zawacki, Data Axle
7. Tailor Messaging For Target Audiences
With the appropriate prompts and information provided to it, generative AI can serve as a valuable starting point for uniquely tailored messaging for your target audience. At the same time, it is important to realize that AI in its current form is just a tool, and overreliance on it could actually take away from your brand recognition, authenticity and consistent messaging. - Bahram Moshrefnoory, Rizer Technology Solutions
8. Do The Research Behind Content
One of the most powerful ways generative AI can be used for content is not in the creation of it, but to do the research behind it. Not doing this is truly a missed opportunity, as AI can provide you with unrealized perspectives on a topic or interest. This can lead to new opportunities for creating content that connects with the motivations of your audience. - Roger Hurni, Off Madison Ave
9. Customize Visuals To Mirror Brand Aesthetics
Incorporating generative AI into content creation offers the opportunity to introduce inventive and distinct marketing and advertising assets, including visuals and graphics crafted to align with your brand. AI-generated visuals can be customized to mirror specific brand aesthetics, resulting in a cohesive appearance across marketing materials. - Jessica Hawthorne-Castro, Hawthorne Advertising
10. Crunch User Data To Get Relevant Ideas
Use a secure generative AI tool to crunch real user data and return relevant, personalized ideas about product recommendations, visual enhancements, unique promotional offers, video storyboards, image descriptions and even chatbot interactions that are personalized based on your unique user data. Just remember to vet the ideas AI generates against your brand strategy and customer insights. - Mary Ann O’Brien, OBI Creative
11. Create Backgrounds For Photos
Generative AI can be a super fun way to create creative backgrounds for photos and other graphical elements to share on social media—and it’s much quicker than using traditional tools. - Jodi Amendola, Amendola Communications
12. Enhance Mundane Campaign Elements
Creative professionals have the essential skills to understand brands and their corresponding audiences. Generative AI can provide foundational ideas that these professionals can breathe life into. The creative process is not linear—AI provides an avenue for this process to unfold. It enhances the mundane, facilitating one-of-a-kind campaigns. - Brock Murray, seoplus+
13. Analyze Your Competitors
Instruct AI to analyze top competitors, examine their traffic-generation methods, and create a blueprint from the insights. Curate content based on these findings. AI aids in generating a content plan as well, serving as a roadmap for your strategy. Remember, AI lacks the human touch. To truly stand out, meticulously edit your content, infusing it with relatable elements. - Qamar Zaman, KISSPR Brand Story Press Release Distribution
14. Create Outlines To Use As A Starting Place
Generative AI is a great tool to use to generate ideas and outlines to use as a starting place. We can get stuck using the same ideas over and over again, whereas AI has essentially unlimited ideas and access to other businesses in the industry. Therefore, it is an excellent source to get an idea from, whether it be for copy or graphics, and then craft it to fit the brand. - Trey Robinson, Story Amplify

title: Council Post: The Imperative For Embracing AI: A Phased Approach
text:
Chase is the CEO of ProAI, an AI-powered platform providing customized tools and advisory to help businesses start, fund and scale.
For decades, small and midsize businesses enjoyed an overall level playing field with larger corporations, largely because labor costs were capped by federal minimum wage standards. However, with the emergence of sophisticated AI and automation technologies, I see this balance of power rapidly shifting.
Large corporations now have the resources to invest heavily in AI and robotics, granting them an insurmountable competitive edge. For example, Amazon Go uses computer vision algorithms and sensors to eliminate cashiers, helping slash labor costs.
In manufacturing, increasingly inexpensive self-learning robots are predicted to soon handle everything from assembly to packaging, greatly reducing production costs. In professional services, many firms are developing AI systems to conduct market analysis and generate deliverables, which can allow them to compete for midsize clients at reduced pricing.
Adopting AI Within Small Businesses
However, while large companies are investing in AI, adopting it enterprise-wide remains a challenge. There is an opportunity for small businesses to gain a competitive edge by rapidly integrating AI before their larger competitors fully roll it out. Quickly implementing autonomous systems, even in their current imperfect state, can help small players seize market share, a strategy noted in The Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton Christensen. AI readiness will eventually become an imperative, but early movers can realize major advantages.
I believe that small businesses simply cannot compete on labor costs anymore. Paying humans to do routine work that algorithms can handle cheaply will make it impossible to match prices and production volumes. This necessitates an urgent strategic shift for small and midsize company leaders.
To stay in the game, smaller organizations must embrace AI today. Therefore, leaders should devote substantial time each week to educating themselves on cutting-edge innovations in artificial intelligence, machine learning and intelligent process automation. While current tools have limitations, they are advancing exponentially. Company executives who monitor these technologies closely will gain the foundational knowledge needed to apply them when the capabilities mature.
In addition to self-directed learning, owners can budget for outside AI advisory services. Specialized consultants can provide customized roadmaps to integrate the latest innovations into operations in ways that maximize value and mitigate risks. The goal should be developing an overarching AI strategy that taps algorithms to amplify human talents.
On a broader scale, small business advocacy groups should push for policies that make AI more accessible. Tax credits, subsidies and partnerships with tech research institutions can help smaller players implement AI. Trade groups should also provide training programs to help entrepreneurs and small company leaders rapidly gain AI fluency.
The window for action is short. Large corporations are already aggressively rolling out next-generation tech, and some are even entering entirely new markets. If small businesses do not re-tool their operations to capitalize on AI, they will likely cede entire market segments to dominant players.
Partnering thoughtfully with AI may represent the best opportunity for main street businesses to sustain their competitiveness as corporations continue automating operations. With pragmatism and vision, I believe that small and midsize companies can prosper in the age of intelligent machines.
Specific Areas Where AI Can Transform Small Business Operations
There are several key functions where deploying AI could make an enormous competitive impact for small businesses across sectors:
Strategic Planning
New resources such as our technology can help small to midsize businesses with market research and business strategy frameworks. Created with expertise from consultants at top firms, these tools bring the same strategies and methods to companies of all sizes and can be a valuable resource for existing business consultants to scale and service new clients.
Marketing And Sales
AI marketing tools can rapidly analyze customer data, detect subtle patterns, forecast demand, optimize pricing and personalize engagement across channels. Small e-commerce companies can use AI recommenders to match products/services to customer interests. These technologies allow smaller players to execute sophisticated sales and marketing strategies cost-effectively.
Accounting And Finance
Automating mundane tasks like bookkeeping, reporting and auditing with AI frees small business owners and financial staff to focus on value-driving work. AI-powered solutions can also help with cash flow forecasting, scenario modeling and data-driven decision-making.
Supply Chain And Logistics
AI supply chain systems can synthesize data from across fragmented operations to optimize inventory, purchasing, delivery routes and warehouse workflows. This allows small manufacturers and retailers to manage scaling complexity efficiently.
Human Resources
AI recruiting tools help smaller employers cost-effectively source and evaluate talent from wider candidate pools. HR analytics dashboards using natural language generation can provide personalized coaching and skills training guidance tailored to each employee.
Information Technology
From predictive maintenance to automated cybersecurity monitoring, AI IT solutions give understaffed small business IT teams enterprise-grade infrastructure oversight. Intelligent networks can self-diagnose issues and resolve them rapidly without needing large dedicated tech teams.
The Way Forward: A Phased Approach To AI Adoption
Balancing urgency with careful planning, here is a path to effectively and incrementally implement AI in stages:
1. Process Analysis And Education
Conduct an in-depth analysis of all key processes and workflows. Identify areas where algorithms could drive the most impact. Continue executive education on AI capabilities relevant to the company's operations.
2. Pilot Implementation
Run controlled AI pilot projects in one to two high-opportunity areas. Measure results closely and fine-tune systems. Use lessons learned to establish governance practices and change management strategies.
3. Comprehensive Rollout
With governance and training programs in place, gradually scale AI across end-to-end operations. Maintain close human oversight and cross-functional collaboration. Continuously assess performance and ethics.
The Bottom Line
The message for small business leaders is clear: To sustain competitiveness as corporations accelerate automation, companies must urgently re-tool operations with AI. By infusing operations with algorithmic intelligence, and keeping humans firmly involved, I am certain that small and midsize players can secure their place in the emerging economy.

title: Council Post: Why A 'Wait And See' Approach To New Tech Can Get Your Company Left Behind
text:
Co-CEO and Founder of Buildout, Inc. a Saas and solution provider that believes that CRE success is broker-led, but tech-enabled.
I find that many people have a strange habit when it comes to new technologies. As a new technology emerges, they react with skepticism—even cynicism. Yet, as it proves itself and becomes part of everyday life, these same skeptics act as though its success were a foregone conclusion, soon taking the advancements for granted and failing to acknowledge their earlier doubts.
Recall how the internet was mocked in the '90s, with news anchors and talk show hosts skeptical at the notion of an "information superhighway." Merely a decade later, they were delivering reports via that very internet. Today, I'm seeing artificial intelligence (AI) undergoing a similar pattern of skepticism and inevitable acceptance. Many view AI with doubt, however, I believe AI differs in its rate of development.
I have personally been following and studying AI for the past five years. Starting in December 2022, my team and I made adopting AI an organization-wide priority. Over the past 13 months, we have adopted AI extensively in every department, and, today, AI answers many of our support questions, helps our developers write code and assists in producing new marketing content. These experiences have taught me that businesses simply can't afford to wait to adopt AI.
Why Organizations Shouldn't Ignore AI
Fourteen months ago, we did not have AI in the way it's discussed and leveraged today. To most, AI likely meant Siri or Alexa. While complex, there were narrow AI applications already deployed across industries; these powered everyday tools such as Google Search, and the average person often didn't realize they were interacting with AI. But now, it's unmistakably and unavoidably present. Has any other technology advanced this swiftly?
This technological revolution is distinct in its blazing pace. Consider this past year’s events: the emergence of a nascent technology, rapid maturation, the rise of numerous formidable competitors, record-breaking growth, industry-wide disruptions, legal battles and global governmental scrutiny—all within a single year. In my view, nothing has progressed this rapidly.
In previous technological revolutions, there was the luxury of time. When the internet gained traction in the '90s, businesses didn't have to immediately migrate online. Similarly, when software transitioned from desktops to the web in the 2000s, or when the iPhone and its app store launched, there was no immediate imperative to adapt. However, companies eventually had to evolve or risk obsolescence at the hands of more agile competitors. Yet, they had years to evaluate the situation and plan their strategies. This has not been the case with AI.
When the internet began captivating the mainstream, innovative early adopters started moving their businesses online. Similarly, we saw brick-and-mortar stores launching e-commerce platforms; companies started interacting with customers through email and online forums; and many businesses created websites for distributing information. We also saw where some even transitioned their entire business to the web. But this shift was gradual, with most having years to adapt. Being online became essential for survival, but it didn't happen overnight.
I believe the emergence of AI should not be treated with the same complacency, and those who embrace it could gain such advantages that slower-moving competitors will struggle to compete. While there are risks to consider, AI can enable companies to provide improved products and services, whether through speed—such as AI agents offering instant support—or by making previously impossible services feasible, such as detecting the onset of diabetes through a short audio recording. Beyond improving offerings, AI can help enhance operational efficiency, potentially reducing costs and prices.
Getting Started With AI
As a business leader, it's important that you proactively stay aware of the developments that are happening every day. I would recommend subscribing to an AI newsletter. As you see opportunities to adopt new solutions, don't make them initiatives for next quarter if you can start testing them out sooner.
Next, I recommend exploring the AI capabilities that are being released in the software you already subscribe to. Your customer relationship management or ticketing system might have already launched AI features that can start saving you hours of work across your teams. Keep in mind that these features might be add-ons that you have to purchase, but don't wait for your account manager to reach out to pitch these to you.
Finally, I suggest doing some recon on what your competitors are doing. You don't want to get left behind. This is especially true if you are running a software company. It's OK if you ended 2023 without incorporating AI into your product, but I believe it's going to be conspicuous if that's the case at the end of 2024.
While the intricacies of AI might be complex, businesses should not be mere spectators. How will you fare against competitors adopting this technology? Can you afford to "wait and see?"

title: How This Under 30-Founded Drink Spiking Prevention Tool Landed A Spot On Forever 21 Shelves
text:
Think this is nice? It’s a version of the weekly Under 30 newsletter and would be even better in your inbox.
As dry January comes to a close, many are facing the decision to stick with water for the long haul or opt for a beer, wine or mixed drink come February 1. But no matter the beverage, this brother-sister duo wants to make sure you’re imbibing safely.
Michael and Shirah Benarde are the cofounders of NightCap, and earned a spot on the 2024 Under 30 Retail & Ecommerce list. NightCap sells hair scrunchies that unfold into drink covers to prevent roofies and other unwanted substances from being dropped in a cup. The idea was born in 2019, when Shirah says her friend was roofied at a college bar and a few weeks later, Shirah had a dream that she could prevent it with a new invention. The next morning, she turned a scrunchie of her own and a pair of her mom’s pantyhose into the first prototype.
“We surveyed 100 women when we started the company and 26% of them said they had their drinks spiked,” says Shirah, 21. “Realizing that it was a problem, that's how we market it now: It's a fun solution to a serious problem.”
With growing education around the topic of drink safety, the two have generated quite the community of customers since their 2020 launch. That year, one of the startup’s TikTok posts brought in $40,000 in sales. In 2021, they landed a spot on Shark Tank, where investor Lori Greneir offered $60,000 for 25% of the business. Their slot on the show got the attention of singer-songwriter Julia Michaels, who then invested $100,000 into the company for 10% ownership. In 2023, they brought in $2 million in revenue.
Today, 50% of revenue is from direct-to-consumer sales, with TikTok being a significant driver. NightCap has 470,000 followers on TikTok, with some videos hitting 20 to 40 million views. Additionally, the startup has focused on strategic partnerships, including one with more than 150 college campuses that buy NightCap products in bulk to hand out to students at fairs and other university events. They’ve also partnered with dating app Bumble, which customized a couple hundred scrunchies to give out to their brand ambassadors, and most recently, retailer Forever 21, which purchased 8,500 scrunchies to sell at 400 retail stores starting this month.
To land the Forever 21 deal, Shirah says she cold-pitched Forever 21 CEO Winnie Park after hearing her speak on a women’s empowerment panel at retail tradeshow ShopTalk last year. “Afterward, we walked up to her and said, ‘You did so amazing, here's a NightCap.’ And immediately she said, ‘Let's get this in the stores.’”
As NightCap continues to grow, Shirah says they’re targeting more partnerships to scale, including music festivals. And they’ve signed deals with multiple bars, which are particularly interested in their disposable sticker covers as an alternative to the scrunchies, she says.

Building a startup can be incredibly stressful. Somewhere between creating pitch decks, managing a team and trying to win over customers, founders might forget that they’re more than just a company. So how do you protect your peace and run a business?
Take a minute to hear from our Under 30 listers about their personal journeys with mental health and how they stay balanced. Up this week: April Koh, a 2018 Consumer Technology Under 30 lister and cofounder of mental healthcare company Spring Health, which has notched a $2.5 billion valuation (and $370 million in venture funding) since it was founded in 2016.
The following has been slightly edited for length and clarity.
The ethos of your business is helping others better their wellbeing. How has this affected your own mental health?
Being a mental health founder is a lot to balance, but the challenges I face are not ones I experience alone. Founders are often caught in a balancing act between being confident that your idea can really create lasting change—maintaining a thick skin when people cast doubt on the company we are building—and having humility to realize when you need to change course. With so much at stake, I sometimes have to remind myself to put on my oxygen mask first, so that I can continue to be as authentic as possible and maintain focus.
Do you have a go-to activity or routine for when you’re feeling down?
I recently became a mom, and having dedicated time with my family has been an essential part of my daily routine. Each day, I spend time with my baby with my phone turned off to make sure I’m present with her. This unplugged time is something I look forward to no matter what else is happening.
I’m also a big proponent of walking as a form of exercise, mental wellness and a time to reflect. You can often find me taking long walks with my noise-canceling headphones. I walk home from work every day and it helps keep me grounded and offers a moment to just think.
What’s your best advice for prioritizing mental health while running a business?
As founders or business leaders, we are constantly met with decisions that need to be made. A big struggle that leaders often have to grapple with is how to cope when things go wrong. An easy way to damage your mental health is to over-blame yourself or feel ashamed when mistakes happen. Try to realize when you are being too hard on yourself and focus on what needs to happen next. Most importantly, don’t lose sight of your purpose because it will continue to be your source of daily motivation.
As a leader, how do you encourage your teams to take charge of their wellbeing?
From the outset, we have been very intentional about living by our mission of delivering a mentally healthy workplace. I really believe in the importance of recovery and recharging. We encourage employees to take their PTO and we remain focused on keeping a mentally safe workplace for everyone.
Do you think the entrepreneurial community does a satisfactory job at talking about mental health? What cultural norms still need to change?
It’s a topic I wish the entrepreneurial community talked about more frequently. Very often when entrepreneurs get together, you’ll hear people talk about their successes. Many times we hear about this 24/7 mentality and unwavering drive for impact. But there is so much that entrepreneurs don’t open up about that we could all benefit greatly from. I think it’s so important for entrepreneurs to talk about their anxieties, fears, hurdles. Perhaps people fear that this vulnerability is a sign of weakness in a space where so many are trying to prove themselves.
Let’s normalize talking about the moments where it feels like everything is falling apart, because no matter how well a business appears to be doing from the outside, I guarantee there are many underlying difficulties that we could all benefit from speaking openly about and learning from others. As a founder, I know firsthand how much we have to juggle, and it’s important that this community emphasizes cultivating mental wellness. The 24/7 mentality can only go so far – just because you burn the candle at both ends doesn’t mean you’re doing it right.

Elon Musk's AI start-up seeks to raise up to $6 billion - FT
The AI race has been heating up with several investors signing big checks for start-ups looking to capitalize on what has captured Silicon Valley's attention over the past year.
Elon Musk's artificial intelligence start-up xAI is in talks to raise up to $6 billion at a proposed valuation of $20 billion, the Financial Times reported on Friday, as the billionaire entrepreneur looks to mount a challenge to OpenAI.
The start-up has been in talks with family offices in Hong Kong and is targeting sovereign wealth funds in the Middle East for the funding, according to the report, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter.
The AI race has been heating up with several investors signing big checks for start-ups looking to capitalize on what has captured Silicon Valley's attention over the past year.
A $6-billion fundraise would be much higher than the $1 billion goal xAI had set last month in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
At $20 billion, xAI's valuation would be a fraction of OpenAI's, but in line with some other peers such as Google-backed Anthropic.
Musk has approached investors in Japan and South Korea for the latest fundraise, the Financial Times reported. His office did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Morgan Stanley is coordinating the fundraise, according to the report. The bank was one of several that helped finance Musk's takeover of social media platform X, formerly known as Twitter.
Last week, Musk denied a report that xAI had secured $500 million in commitments from investors toward a $1 billion funding goal.
The CEO of Tesla has been vocal about his plans to build safer AI. Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015, but stepped down from its board in 2018.
Last year, xAI launched "Grok", a chatbot rivaling OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Musk also warned about developing AI and robotics outside Tesla, earlier this month, unless he gets more voting control at the electric-vehicle maker. He said he would be uncomfortable building Tesla into an AI leader unless he had 25% voting control.
Thanks to the popularity of ChatGPT, the AI industry has been a rare bright spot in a subdued start-up funding environment.
Anthropic and Microsoft-backed Inflection AI have also raised funds in recent months.

title: Why AI Methods Need Heightened Security
text:
AI is increasingly pervasive and with the acceleration in the past twelve months of Large Language Models (LLMs) and of generative AI tools like Chat GPT, AI models are exploding everywhere.
According to most recent market reports, the AI market is expected to grow in value from $11.3 billion in 2023 to $51.8 billion by 2028. With ChatGPT already setting a record as the fastest-growing internet app in our history, it is imperative to recognize the increasingly vulnerabilities and risks of AI models growth patterns. It is already estimated there are billions of AI models globally, although Gartner recently revealed that, on average, only 54% of AI projects make it from pilot to production. Other credible reports say the numbers getting to production are less than 75%, either way - no one can discount the risk of AI models being attacked.
AI data is very vulnerable to attacks and deficiencies, such as data poisoning by malicious actors or data quality issues introduced during training which can adversely affect model performance. Also AI models can be exploited by both naturally occurring and malicious inputs that can produce incorrect outcomes at inference, and leak sensitive data, presenting security and data privacy risks. In addition, AI Models have inherent deficiencies due to: unpredictable long-tailed edge cases and are also susceptible to issues of: security, privacy, robustness, bias, explainability, financial and reputational risk exposure.
As a result of these security risk factors, the AI security market is exploding. According to Mordor Intelligence, the security market is estimated at USD $25.22 billion in 2024, and is expected to reach USD $60.24 billion by 2029, growing at a CAGR of 19.02% during the forecast period (2024-2029). Implementing machine learning with AI enables threats and malware to be proactively prevented rather than only detected. This is expected to create a major market growth opportunity for AI in the security market during the forecast period.
Unfortunately, attackers are incredibly creative in finding ways to skew AI data models by corrupting the data used to train AI models. This can involve adding malicious data, changing data or infecting streaming data during model update cycles. This is often called poisoning and being able to protect, vet and have constant visibility of the AI models is critical to manage risk. We are currently experiencing security risks of generative AI lowering the barrier for new threat actors to conduct sophisticated and scalable attacks, from deep fakes to high-fidelity phishing emails and AI-generated ransomware.
One of the most innovative Canadian AI companies pioneering to reduce the AI/ML model risks is TrojAI. Their vision is to become the most trusted name in AI security by enabling the responsible deployment of safe and secure AI technology. Founded in in June 2019 by Dr. James Stewart and Stephen Goddard, as a result of Dr. Stewart’s concerns with the increasing security and risk vulnerabilities that were emerging from the rapid adoption of AI. Now venture backed with strong VC’s including Flying Fish out of Seattle, Build Ventures and Concrete Ventures both of Halifax, Techstars, and the New Brunswick Innovation Foundation, they are working to further commercialize their AI Software platform. The company has blended talent disciplines from cybersecurity and deep learning and they are now entering their fifth year of software development of their secure AI risk platform that covers computer vision, natural language processing, machine learning and LLM’s.
Organizations are under immense pressure to develop innovative strategies and new products to take advantage of the AI muscle power. Research is also showing the value that AI brings but security teams are scrambling for real solutions to protect their organizations from the security threats and risks that enterprises can be exposed to through their use of AI.
Solutions like TrojAI, along with Calypso and Robust Intelligence, have all been working on this big problem since late 2018 or early 2019. Customers purchasing AI Security solutions are typically large or mid-market enterprises but as AI advances into smaller business markets, all organizations that are building a foundation of AI into their operating processes will have to increase their focus on AI Security.
According to GapGemini, approximately 60% of organizations believe that they would be unable to identify critical threats without the use of advanced artificial intelligence technologies. The late fall release of the US AI Executive Order can only help to increase the focus on designing and building more secure and safer AI models from the bad actor explosion.
But the reality is passing new laws takes time, and we need to have a heightened awareness and sense of urgency of board directors and c-suite officers asking the right questions to proactively manage AI cyber security risks.
Three questions for board directors and c-suite to get started on I recommend are:
- What are the methods and controls that are being used to prevent malware from poisoning any AI model training sets?
- Have all High risk application AI algorithms been tested by a 3rd-party that can confirm its ability to detect and prevent malware?
- What are the protections against the new attack surface of generative AI — including data poisoning and prompt injection?
In summary, leaders must accelerate their focus on prevention and develop proactive measures to safeguard AI models from adversarial attacks, data breaches, and unauthorized access. This includes techniques such as: secure AI model development and execution end to end, encryption of sensitive data, implementing robust authentication mechanisms and ensuring data flows are monitored with real-time risk detection methods, anything less - will likely see companies with more data privacy breaches, ransom attacks, and of course legal bills.
Companies like TrojAI, a Canadian company, I am proud to say is pioneering and making a valuable AI security contribution, another Unicorn in the making.
